body.text: Arthaviniścayasūtram |
body.translated_text: <s>Arthaviniścayasūtra</s> (The Sūtra on the Ascertainment of Meaning)

body.text: śrīmañjugurave(śriye) namaḥ |
body.translated_text: Homage to the glorious <s>Mañjuguru</s> (<s>Mañjuśrī</s>).

body.text: bhagavānāha - kaścāsau bhikṣavo 'rthaviniścayo nāma dharmaparyāyaḥ? yaduktam - pañca skandhāḥ | pañcopādānaskandhāḥ | aṣṭādaśa dhātavaḥ | dvādaśāyatanāni | dvādaśāṅgaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ | catvāri āryasatyāni | dvāviṃśati indriyāṇi | catvāri dhyānāni | [catasra ārūpyasamāpattayaḥ] | catvāro brahmavihārāḥ | catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ | catasraḥ samādhibhāvanāḥ | catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni | catvāri samyakprahāṇāni | catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ | pañcendriyāṇi | pañca balāni | sapta bodhyaṅgāni | āryāṣṭāṅgamārgaḥ | ṣoḍaśākārā ānāpānānusmṛtiḥ | catvāri srotāpattyaṅgāni | daśa tathāgatabalāni catvāri vaiśāradyāni | catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ | aṣṭādaśa āveṇikabuddhadharmāḥ | dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇāni | aśītyanuvyañjanāni | ayaṃ bhikṣavo 'rthaviniścayasya dharmaparyāyasyoddeśaḥ ||
body.translated_text: The Blessed One said: 'And what, monks, is this <s>dharma</s>-discourse called the Ascertainment of Meaning? As has been stated: the five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates); the five <s>upādānaskandhas</s> (aggregates of clinging); the eighteen <s>dhātus</s> (elements); the twelve <s>āyatanas</s> (sense bases); the twelve-limbed <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination); the four <s>āryasatyas</s> (noble truths); the twenty-two <s>indriyas</s> (faculties); the four <s>dhyānas</s> (meditative absorptions); the four <s>ārūpyasamāpattis</s> (formless attainments); the four <s>brahmavihāras</s> (divine abodes); the four <s>pratisaṃvids</s> (analytical knowledges); the four cultivations of <s>samādhi</s> (concentration); the four <s>smṛtyupasthānas</s> (foundations of mindfulness); the four <s>samyakprahāṇas</s> (right exertions); the four <s>ṛddhipādas</s> (bases of supernatural power); the five <s>indriyas</s> (spiritual faculties); the five <s>balas</s> (powers); the seven <s>bodhyaṅgas</s> (factors of awakening); the noble eightfold path (<s>āryāṣṭāṅgamārga</s>); the sixteen aspects of <s>ānāpānasmṛti</s> (mindfulness of breathing); the four factors of stream-entry (<s>srotāpattyaṅga</s>); the ten powers of the <s>Tathāgata</s> (<s>tathāgatabala</s>); the four <s>vaiśāradyas</s> (fearlessnesses); the four <s>pratisaṃvids</s> (analytical knowledges); the eighteen <s>āveṇikabuddhadharmas</s> (distinctive qualities of a Buddha); the thirty-two marks of a great being (<s>mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa</s>); the eighty minor marks (<s>anuvyañjana</s>). This, monks, is the outline of the <s>dharma</s>-discourse called the Ascertainment of Meaning.'

body.text: (1) tatra bhikṣavaḥ katame pañca skandhāḥ? tadyathā - rūpaskandhaḥ | vedanāskandhaḥ | saṃjñāskandhaḥ | saṃskāraskandhaḥ | vijñānaskandhaḥ | ime bhikṣavaḥ pañca skandhāḥ ||
body.translated_text: (1) 'Therein, monks, what are the five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates)? They are: <s>rūpaskandha</s> (aggregate of form), <s>vedanāskandha</s> (aggregate of feeling), <s>saṃjñāskandha</s> (aggregate of perception), <s>saṃskāraskandha</s> (aggregate of volitional formations), <s>vijñānaskandha</s> (aggregate of consciousness). These, monks, are the five <s>skandhas</s>.'

body.text: (2) tatra bhikṣavaḥ katame pañcopādānaskandhāḥ? tadyathā - rūpopādānaskandhaḥ | vedanopādānaskandhaḥ | saṃjñopādānaskandhaḥ | saṃskāropādānaskandhaḥ | vijñānopādānaskandhaḥ | ime bhikṣavaḥ pañcopādānaskandhāḥ ||
body.translated_text: (2) 'Therein, monks, what are the five <s>upādānaskandhas</s> (aggregates of clinging)? They are: <s>rūpopādānaskandha</s> (aggregate of clinging to form), <s>vedanopādānaskandha</s> (aggregate of clinging to feeling), <s>saṃjñopādānaskandha</s> (aggregate of clinging to perception), <s>saṃskāropādānaskandha</s> (aggregate of clinging to volitional formations), <s>vijñānopādānaskandha</s> (aggregate of clinging to consciousness). These, monks, are the five <s>upādānaskandhas</s>.'

body.text: (3) tatra bhikṣavaṃ katame 'ṣṭadaśa dhātavaḥ? tadyathā - cakṣudhātuḥ | rūpadhātuḥ | cakṣurvijñānadhātuḥ | śrotadhātuḥ | śabdadhātuḥ | śrotravijñānadhātuḥ | ghrāṇadhātuḥ | gandhadhātuḥ | ghrāṇavijñānadhātuḥ | jihvādhātuḥ | rasadhātuḥ | jihvāvijñānadhātuḥ | kāyadhātuḥ | sparśadhātuḥ | kāyavijñānadhātuḥ | manodhātuḥ | dharmadhātuḥ | manovijñānadhātuḥ | ime bhikṣava ucyante 'ṣṭādaśa dhātavaḥ ||
body.translated_text: (3) 'Therein, monks, what are the eighteen <s>dhātus</s> (elements)? They are: <s>cakṣudhātu</s> (eye element), <s>rūpadhātu</s> (form element), <s>cakṣurvijñānadhātu</s> (eye-consciousness element); <s>śrotradhātu</s> (ear element), <s>śabdadhātu</s> (sound element), <s>śrotravijñānadhātu</s> (ear-consciousness element); <s>ghrāṇadhātu</s> (nose element), <s>gandhadhātu</s> (smell element), <s>ghrāṇavijñānadhātu</s> (nose-consciousness element); <s>jihvādhātu</s> (tongue element), <s>rasadhātu</s> (taste element), <s>jihvāvijñānadhātu</s> (tongue-consciousness element); <s>kāyadhātu</s> (body element), <s>sparśadhātu</s> (touch element), <s>kāyavijñānadhātu</s> (body-consciousness element); <s>manodhātu</s> (mind element), <s>dharmadhātu</s> (dharma element), <s>manovijñānadhātu</s> (mind-consciousness element). These, monks, are called the eighteen <s>dhātus</s>.'

body.text: (4) tatra bhikṣavaḥ katamāni dvādaśāyatanāni? yaduta cakṣuradhyātmikamāyatanam | rūpamadhyātmikamāyatanam | śrotramadhyātmikamāyatanam | śabdo bāhyamāyatanam | ghrāṇamadhyātmikamāyatanam | gandho bāhyamāyatanam | jihvā adhyātmikamāyatanam | raso bāhyamāyatanam | kāyo 'dhyātmikamāyatanam | sparśo bāhyamāyatanam | mana adhyātmikamāyatanam | dharmo bāhyamāyatanam | imāni bhikṣava ucyante dvādaśāyatanāni ||
body.translated_text: (4) 'Therein, monks, what are the twelve <s>āyatanas</s> (sense bases)? They are: the eye as an internal sense base, form as an external sense base; the ear as an internal sense base, sound as an external sense base; the nose as an internal sense base, smell as an external sense base; the tongue as an internal sense base, taste as an external sense base; the body as an internal sense base, touch as an external sense base; the mind as an internal sense base, <s>dharmas</s> as an external sense base. These, monks, are called the twelve <s>āyatanas</s>.'

body.text: (5) tatra bhikṣavaḥ katamo dvādaśāṅgaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ? avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ | saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam | vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam | nāmarūpapratyayaṃ ṣaḍāyatanam | ṣaḍāyatanapratyayaḥ sparśaḥ | sparśapratyayā vedanā | vedanāpratyayā tṛṣṇā | tṛṣṇāpratyayādupādānam | upādānapratyayādbhavaḥ | bhavapratyayājjātiḥ | jātipratyayā jarāmaraṇaśokaparidevaduḥkhadaurmana

children.translated_text: Thus arises the entire great mass of suffering. From the cessation of <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) comes the cessation of <s>saṃskāras</s> (volitional formations); from the cessation of <s>saṃskāras</s> comes the cessation of <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness); from the cessation of <s>vijñāna</s> comes the cessation of <s>nāmarūpa</s> (name-and-form); from the cessation of <s>nāmarūpa</s> comes the cessation of the six <s>āyatanas</s> (sense bases); from the cessation of the six <s>āyatanas</s> comes the cessation of <s>sparśa</s> (contact); from the cessation of <s>sparśa</s> comes the cessation of <s>vedanā</s> (feeling); from the cessation of <s>vedanā</s> comes the cessation of <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving); from the cessation of <s>tṛṣṇā</s> comes the cessation of <s>upādāna</s> (clinging); from the cessation of <s>upādāna</s> comes the cessation of <s>bhava</s> (becoming); from the cessation of <s>bhava</s> comes the cessation of <s>jāti</s> (birth); from the cessation of <s>jāti</s>, <s>jarāmaraṇa</s> (aging and death), <s>śoka</s> (sorrow), <s>parideva</s> (lamentation), <s>duḥkha</s> (suffering), <s>daurmanasya</s> (displeasure), and <s>upāyāsa</s> (despair) cease. Thus comes the cessation of the entire great mass of suffering.'

body.translated_text: (5) 'Therein, monks, what is the twelve-limbed <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination)? (a) tatra katamā avidyā? yattatpūrvānte 'jñānam | aparānte 'jñānam | pūrvā(ntā) parānte 'jñānam | adhyātma ajñānam | bahirdhā ajñānam | adhyātmabahirdhā ajñānam | karmaṇyajñānam | vipāke 'jñānam | karmavipāke 'jñānam | sukṛte 'jñānam | duṣkṛte 'jñānam | sukṛtaduṣkṛteṣu dharmeṣvajñānam | hetāvajñānam | phale 'jñānam | hetuphale 'jñānam | hetusamutpanneṣu dharmeṣvajñānam | pratītyasamutpāde 'jñānam | pratītyasamutpanneṣu dharmeṣvajñānam | buddhe 'jñānam | dharme 'jñānam | saṃghe 'jñānam | duḥkhe 'jñānam | samudaye 'jñānam | nirodhe 'jñānam | mārge 'jñānam | kuśale 'jñānam | akuśale 'jñānam | kuśalākuśaleṣu dharmeṣvajñānam | sāvadye 'jñānam | anavadye 'jñānam | sāvadyānavadyeṣu dharmeṣvajñānam | sevitavye 'jñānam | asevitavye 'jñānam | sevitavyāsevitavyeṣu dharmeṣvajñānam | sāsrave 'jñānam | anāsrave 'jñānam | sāsravānāsraveṣu dharmeṣvajñānam | saṃskṛte 'jñānam | asaṃskṛte 'jñānam | saṃskṛtāsaṃskṛteṣu

body.translated_text: (a) Therein, what is <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance)? It is ignorance regarding the past; ignorance regarding the future; ignorance regarding both past and future; ignorance regarding what is internal; ignorance regarding what is external; ignorance regarding both internal and external; ignorance regarding <s>karma</s> (action); ignorance regarding <s>vipāka</s> (ripening/result); ignorance regarding both <s>karma</s> and its <s>vipāka</s>; ignorance regarding what is well-done; ignorance regarding what is ill-done; ignorance regarding <s>dharmas</s> both well-done and ill-done; ignorance regarding cause; ignorance regarding result; ignorance regarding cause and result; ignorance regarding <s>dharmas</s> arisen from causes; ignorance regarding <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination); ignorance regarding <s>dharmas</s> arisen through dependent origination; ignorance regarding the <s>Buddha</s>; ignorance regarding the <s>Dharma</s>; ignorance regarding the <s>Saṃgha</s>; ignorance regarding <s>duḥkha</s> (suffering); ignorance regarding <s>samudaya</s> (origination); ignorance regarding <s>nirodha</s> (cessation); ignorance regarding <s>mārga</s> (the path); ignorance regarding what is wholesome (<s>kuśala</s>); ignorance regarding what is unwholesome (<s>akuśala</s>); ignorance regarding <s>dharmas</s> both wholesome and unwholesome; ignorance regarding what is blameworthy (<s>sāvadya</s>); ignorance regarding what is blameless (<s>anavadya</s>); ignorance regarding <s>dharmas</s> both blameworthy and blameless; ignorance regarding what should be cultivated (<s>sevitavya</s>); ignorance regarding what should not be cultivated (<s>asevitavya</s>); ignorance regarding <s>dharmas</s> both to be cultivated and not cultivated; ignorance regarding what has defilements (<s>sāsrava</s>); ignorance regarding what is without defilements (<s>anāsrava</s>); ignorance regarding <s>dharmas</s> both with and without defilements; ignorance regarding the conditioned (<s>saṃskṛta</s>); ignorance regarding the unconditioned (<s>asaṃskṛta</s>); ignorance regarding <s>dharmas</s> both conditioned and unconditioned; ignorance regarding the past; ignorance regarding the future; ignorance regarding the present; ignorance regarding <s>dharmas</s> past, future, and present. Or, regarding the six sense-bases of contact (<s>sparśāyatana</s>), the absence of true knowledge, non-seeing, non-comprehension, darkness, delusion, the blindness of ignorance — this is called <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance).

body.text: (ā) avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārā iti | saṃskārāḥ katame? trayaḥ saṃskārāḥ - kāyasaṃskāraḥ vāksaṃskāraḥ manaḥsaṃskāraśca | tatra kāyasaṃskāraḥ katamaḥ? āśvāsaḥ praśvāsaḥ | kāyiko hyeṣa dharmaḥ, kāyaniśritaḥ kāyapratibaddhaḥ | kāyaṃ niśritya vartate | tasmādāśvāsapraśvāsāḥ kāyasaṃskāra ityucyate || vāksaṃskāraḥ katamaḥ? vitarkayitvā vicārayitvā vācaṃ bhāṣate, nāvitarkayitvā, nāvicārya | tasmādvitarkavicāro vāksaṃskāra ityucyate || manaḥsaṃskāraḥ katamaḥ? raktasya yā cetanā, cittasya ca, tenāsya yā cetanā | caitasiko hyeṣa dharmaḥ | cittaniśritaḥ cittapratibaddhaḥ | cittaṃ niśritya pravartate | tasmāccetanā manaḥsaṃskāra ityucyate ||
body.translated_text: (ā) 'Conditioned by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) are the <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations).' What are <s>saṃskāras</s>? There are three <s>saṃskāras</s>: the bodily formation (<s>kāyasaṃskāra</s>), the vocal formation (<s>vāksaṃskāra</s>), and the mental formation (<s>manaḥsaṃskāra</s>). Therein, what is the bodily formation? It is inhalation (<s>āśvāsa</s>) and exhalation (<s>praśvāsa</s>). For this is a bodily <s>dharma</s>, dependent on the body, bound to the body; it occurs in dependence on the body. Therefore, inhalation and exhalation are called the bodily formation. What is the vocal formation? Having applied initial thought (<s>vitarka</s>) and sustained thought (<s>vicāra</s>), one speaks — not without initial thought, not without sustained thought. Therefore, initial thought and sustained thought are called the vocal formation. What is the mental formation? The volition (<s>cetanā</s>) of one who is attached, and of the mind, the volition that belongs to it. For this is a mental <s>dharma</s>, dependent on the mind, bound to the mind; it occurs in dependence on the mind. Therefore, volition is called the mental formation.

body.text: (i) saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānamiti | vijñānaṃ katamat? ṣaḍ vijñānakāyāḥ | katame ṣaṭ? tadyathā - cakṣurvijñānam | śrotravijñānam | ghrāṇavijñānam | jihvāvijñānam | kāyavijñānam | manovijñānam | ime ṣaḍ vijñānakāyāḥ ||
body.translated_text: (i) 'Conditioned by the <s>saṃskāras</s> (formations) is <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness).' What is <s>vijñāna</s>? The six groups of consciousness (<s>vijñānakāya</s>). Which six? Namely: eye-consciousness (<s>cakṣurvijñāna</s>), ear-consciousness (<s>śrotravijñāna</s>), nose-consciousness (<s>ghrāṇavijñāna</s>), tongue-consciousness (<s>jihvāvijñāna</s>), body-consciousness (<s>kāyavijñāna</s>), and mind-consciousness (<s>manovijñāna</s>). These are the six groups of consciousness.

children.translated_text: ) is 'name.' What is 'form' (<s>rūpa</s>)? Whatever form there is — it consists of the four great elements (<s>mahābhūta</s>) and what is derived from the four great elements. Namely: the earth element (<s>pṛthivīdhātu</s>), the water element (<s>abdhātu</s>), the fire element (<s>tejodhātu</s>), and the wind element (<s>vāyudhātu</s>). What is the earth element? Heaviness and hardness. What is the water element? Fluidity and moisture. What is the fire element? Heat and maturation. What is the wind element? Contraction, expansion, and the quality of light movement. This 'form' together with the preceding 'name' — combining both into one — is called <s>nāmarūpa</s> (name-and-form).

body.translated_text: (ī) 'Conditioned by <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) is <s>nāmarūpa</s> (name-and-form).' Therein, <s>nāmarūpa</s> — 'name' (<s>nāma</s>) consists of the four formless aggregates (<s>skandhas</s>). Which four? The aggregate of feeling (<s>vedanāskandha</s>), the aggregate of perception (<s>saṃjñāskandha</s>), the aggregate of formations (<s>saṃskāraskandha</s>), and the aggregate of consciousness (<s>vijñānaskandha</s>). body.text: (u) nāmarūpapratyayaṃ ṣaḍāyatanamiti | ṣaḍāyatanaṃ katamat? cakṣurāyatanam | śrotrāyatanam | ghrāṇāyatanam | jihvāyatanam | kāyāyatanam | manaāyatanam | idamucyate ṣaḍāyatanam ||
body.translated_text: (u) 'Conditioned by <s>nāmarūpa</s> (name-and-form) is <s>ṣaḍāyatana</s> (the six sense-bases).' What is <s>ṣaḍāyatana</s>? The eye sense-base (<s>cakṣurāyatana</s>), the ear sense-base (<s>śrotrāyatana</s>), the nose sense-base (<s>ghrāṇāyatana</s>), the tongue sense-base (<s>jihvāyatana</s>), the body sense-base (<s>kāyāyatana</s>), and the mind sense-base (<s>manaāyatana</s>). These are called the six sense-bases.

body.text: (ū) ṣaḍāyatanapratyayaḥ sparśa iti | sparśaḥ katamaḥ? ṣaṭ sparśakāyāḥ - cakṣusaṃsparśaḥ | śrotrasaṃsparśaḥ | ghrāṇasaṃsparśaḥ | jihvāsaṃsparśaḥ | kāyasaṃsparśaḥ | manaḥsaṃsparśaḥ |(ayamucyate sparśaḥ) ||
body.translated_text: The six sense-bases (<s>ṣaḍāyatana</s>) are the condition for contact (<s>sparśa</s>). What is <s>sparśa</s> (contact)? There are six groups of contact: eye-contact (<s>cakṣusaṃsparśa</s>), ear-contact (<s>śrotrasaṃsparśa</s>), nose-contact (<s>ghrāṇasaṃsparśa</s>), tongue-contact (<s>jihvāsaṃsparśa</s>), body-contact (<s>kāyasaṃsparśa</s>), and mind-contact (<s>manaḥsaṃsparśa</s>). This is called contact (<s>sparśa</s>).

body.text: (e) sparśapratyayā vedanā | vedanā katamā? ṣaḍ vedanāḥ | katame(māḥ?)ṣaṭ? cakṣuḥsaṃsparśajā vedanā sukhā duḥkhā aduḥkhāsukhā ca | śrotrasaṃsparśajā vedanā sukhā duḥkhā aduḥkhāsukhā ca | ghrāṇasaṃsparśajā vedanā sukhā duḥkhā aduḥkhāsukhā ca | jihvāsaṃsparśajā vedanā sukhā duḥkhā aduḥkhāsukhā ca | kāyasaṃsparśajā vedanā sukhā duḥkhā aduḥkhāsukhā ca | manaḥsaṃsparśajā vedanā sukhā duḥkhā aduḥkhāsukhā ca | iyamucyate vedanā ||
body.translated_text: Contact (<s>sparśa</s>) is the condition for feeling (<s>vedanā</s>). What is <s>vedanā</s> (feeling)? There are six feelings. Which six? Feeling born of eye-contact—pleasant (<s>sukhā</s>), painful (<s>duḥkhā</s>), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant (<s>aduḥkhāsukhā</s>); feeling born of ear-contact—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant; feeling born of nose-contact—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant; feeling born of tongue-contact—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant; feeling born of body-contact—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant; feeling born of mind-contact—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. This is called feeling (<s>vedanā</s>).

body.text: (o) vedanāpratyayā tṛṣṇā | katamā tṛṣṇā? ṣaṭ tṛṣṇākāyāḥ | katame ṣaṭ? rūpatṛṣṇā | śabdatṛṣṇā | gandhatṛṣṇā | rasatṛṣṇā | sparśatṛṣṇā | dharmatṛṣṇā |(iyamucyate tṛṣṇā) ||
body.translated_text: Feeling (<s>vedanā</s>) is the condition for craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>). What is <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving)? There are six groups of craving. Which six? Craving for form (<s>rūpatṛṣṇā</s>), craving for sound (<s>śabdatṛṣṇā</s>), craving for smell (<s>gandhatṛṣṇā</s>), craving for taste (<s>rasatṛṣṇā</s>), craving for touch (<s>sparśatṛṣṇā</s>), and craving for mental objects (<s>dharmatṛṣṇā</s>). This is called craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>).

body.text: (ka) tṛṣṇāpratyayamupādānam | upādānaṃ katamat? catvāri upādānāni | katamāni catvāri? tṛṣṇopādānam | śīlavratopādānam | ātmavedanopādānam | (idamucyate upādānam) ||
body.translated_text: Craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) is the condition for clinging (<s>upādāna</s>). What is <s>upādāna</s> (clinging)? There are four types of clinging. Which four? Clinging to craving (<s>tṛṣṇopādāna</s>), clinging to rules and vows (<s>śīlavratopādāna</s>), and clinging to the doctrine of self (<s>ātmavedanopādāna</s>). This is called clinging (<s>upādāna</s>).

children.text: ) ākāśānantyāyatanam | vijñānānantyāyatanam | ākiṃcanyāyatanam | naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanam || ārūpiṇāṃ devānāṃ cittamātramadhyāyināṃ cāturvidhā upapattiḥ | ayamucyate upādānapratyayo bhavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The sphere of infinite space (<s>ākāśānantyāyatana</s>), the sphere of infinite consciousness (<s>vijñānānantyāyatana</s>), the sphere of nothingness (<s>ākiṃcanyāyatana</s>), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (<s>naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana</s>). For the formless gods who meditate on mind-only, there is a fourfold mode of rebirth. This is called existence (<s>bhava</s>) conditioned by clinging (<s>upādāna</s>).

body.translated_text: Clinging (<s>upādāna</s>) is the condition for existence (<s>bhava</s>). What is <s>bhava</s> (existence)? There are three forms of existence. Which three? Existence in the desire realm (<s>kāmabhava</s>), existence in the form realm (<s>rūpabhava</s>), and existence in the formless realm (<s>ārūpyabhava</s>). Among these, what is existence in the desire realm? Namely: the hells (<s>naraka</s>), animals and hungry ghosts (<s>tiryañca</s>, <s>preta</s>), <s>asuras</s>, and the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm. Namely, there are eight great hells. Which eight? The hot great hells: <s>Saṃjīva</s> (Reviving), <s>Kālasūtra</s> (Black Thread), <s>Saṃghāta</s> (Crushing), the two <s>Raurava</s>s (Screaming), <s>Tapana</s> (Burning), <s>Pratāpana</s> (Great Burning), and <s>Avīci</s> (Uninterrupted). These are the great hells. The [cold hells are]: <s>Arbuda</s>, <s>Nirarbuda</s>, <s>Aṭaṭa</s>, <s>Hahava</s>, <s>Huhuva</s>, <s>Utpala</s>, <s>Padma</s>, and <s>Mahāpadma</s>. Which are the six [classes of] gods? The gods of the <s>Cāturmahārājika</s> (Four Great Kings), <s>Trāyastriṃśa</s> (Thirty-three), <s>Yāma</s>, <s>Tuṣita</s>, <s>Nirmāṇarati</s> (Delighting in Creation), and <s>Paranirmitavaśavartin</s> (Controlling Others' Creations). Among these, what is existence in the form realm? Namely: <s>Brahmakāyika</s>, <s>Brahmapurohita</s>, <s>Mahābrahmā</s>, <s>Parīttābha</s> (Limited Light), <s>Apramāṇābha</s> (Immeasurable Light), <s>Ābhāsvara</s> (Streaming Light), <s>Parīttaśubha</s> (Limited Virtue), <s>Apramāṇaśubha</s> (Immeasurable Virtue), <s>Śubhakṛtsna</s> (Total Virtue), <s>Anabhraka</s> (Cloudless), <s>Puṇyaprasava</s> (Merit-born), <s>Abṛha</s>, <s>Atapa</s> (Without Heat), <s>Sudarśana</s> (Fair-seeing), and <s>Akaniṣṭha</s> (Highest). What are the formless realms (<s>ārūpyadhātu</s>)?

body.text: (ga) bhavapratyayā jātiriti | jātiḥ katamāḥ? yā teṣāṃ teṣāṃ sattvānāṃ tasmiṃstasmin sattvanikāye jātiḥ, saṃjātiḥ, avakrāntiḥ, abhinirvṛttiḥ, skandhānāṃ prādurbhāvaḥ, āyatanānāṃ pratilambhaḥ, jīvitendriyasyodbhavaḥ |(iyamucyate jātiḥ |) ||
body.translated_text: Existence (<s>bhava</s>) is the condition for birth (<s>jāti</s>). What is <s>jāti</s> (birth)? It is the birth of those various beings in those various classes of beings—birth, origination, descent [into a womb], manifestation, the appearance of the aggregates (<s>skandha</s>), the acquisition of the sense-bases (<s>āyatana</s>), and the arising of the life-faculty (<s>jīvitendriya</s>). This is called birth (<s>jāti</s>).

body.text: (gha) (jātipratyayaṃ jarāmaraṇam | jarā katamā?) nikāyasabhāgatāyāstasyā yat khālityaṃ pālityaṃ valīpracuratā jīrṇatā bhugnatā kub jagopānasīvakratā khurukhuruśvāsapraśvāsaśca tilakālakopahatagātratā purataḥ prāgbhārakāyatā daṇḍāvaṣṭambhatā indriyāṇāṃ paripākaḥ paribhedaḥ saṃbhārāṇāṃ purāṇībhāvo jarjarībhāvaḥ dhandhatvaṃ mandatvaṃ hāniḥ parihāṇiḥ | iyamucyate jarā || tatra maraṇaṃ katamat? yatteṣāṃ sattvānāṃ tasmācchavikāyāccyutiḥ cyavanatā bhedo 'ntardhānaṃ maraṇaṃ kālakriyā āyuṣo hāniḥ uṣmaṇo hāniḥ jīvitendriyasya nirodhaḥ skandhānāṃ nikṣepaḥ | idamucyate maraṇam || yadetanmaraṇaṃ pūrvikā ca jarā, tadubhayamekatrābhisaṃkṣipya jarāmaraṇamityucyate || ayaṃ bhikṣavo dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpādasyāyaṃ vibhaṅga iti ||
body.translated_text: (d) <s>Jāti</s> (birth) is the condition for <s>jarāmaraṇa</s> (aging and death). What is <s>jarā</s> (aging)? Of the class-continuum (<s>nikāyasabhāgatā</s>), that which is: balding, greying, abundance of wrinkles, decrepitude, being bent over, being stooped and bent like a rafter, breathing with wheezing and gasping, a body afflicted with spots and moles, the body bent forward and leaning, reliance on a walking stick, the maturing and deterioration of the sense faculties, the wearing out and crumbling of the bodily constituents, slowness, dullness, decline, and diminishment—this is called <s>jarā</s> (aging). Therein, what is <s>maraṇa</s> (death)? That which, for those beings, is the falling away from that body of living beings, the passing away, dissolution, disappearance, death, the making of time, loss of lifespan, loss of bodily warmth, the cessation of the life faculty (<s>jīvitendriya</s>), the laying down of the <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates)—this is called <s>maraṇa</s> (death). This death together with the preceding aging—these two, combined under one heading, are called <s>jarāmaraṇa</s> (aging and death). This, monks, is the analysis (<s>vibhaṅga</s>) of the twelve-limbed <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination).'

children.translated_text: Even one afflicted by <s>kleśas</s> (defilements), by cultivating this path, before long attains the cessation of all suffering and, reaching the city of <s>nirvāṇa</s>, obtains complete peace.' These, monks, are the four <s>āryasatyas</s> (noble truths).

body.translated_text: (6) 'Therein, what are the four <s>āryasatyas</s> (noble truths)? They are: the noble truth of <s>duḥkha</s> (suffering), the noble truth of the origin of <s>duḥkha</s>, the noble truth of the cessation of <s>duḥkha</s>, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of <s>duḥkha</s>. Therein, what is the noble truth of <s>duḥkha</s>? Namely: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, separation from what is dear is suffering, association with what is not dear is suffering; <s>rūpa</s> (form) is suffering, <s>vedanā</s> (feeling) is suffering, <s>saṃjñā</s> (perception) is suffering, <s>saṃskāras</s> (volitional formations) are suffering, <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) is suffering; and whatever is sought but not obtained—that too is suffering. In brief, the five <s>upādānaskandhas</s> (aggregates of clinging) are suffering. This is called the noble truth of <s>duḥkha</s>. Therein, what is the noble truth of the origin of <s>duḥkha</s>? Namely: this <s>tṛṣṇā</s> (craving), which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and passion, finding pleasure here and there—this is called the noble truth of the origin of <s>duḥkha</s>. Therein, what is the noble truth of the cessation of <s>duḥkha</s>? That which is the complete abandoning of this very <s>tṛṣṇā</s>—which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and passion, finding pleasure here and there—the letting go, the relinquishing, the exhaustion, the dispassion, the cessation, the pacification, the disappearance—this is called the noble truth of the cessation of <s>duḥkha</s>. Therein, what is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of <s>duḥkha</s>? Namely, the <s>āryāṣṭāṅgamārga</s> (noble eightfold path), [beginning] with right view (<s>samyagdṛṣṭi</s>) and so forth. It is as if some man, overcome by fever, were to approach a physician who is skilled in his craft and learned in the scriptures, and say: "I am in a state of unrest from fever; I desire a medicine to be prescribed for its relief." That physician would first ask about the cause (<s>nidāna</s>): "What have you eaten and drunk?" The sick man would tell him: "I ate yogurt and cucumber, and drank buttermilk with my food and drink." That physician, having diagnosed the condition, would prescribe a medicine. Just so, virtuous ones, tormented by the great fever of birth and the rest, approach the great physician of minds, the greatly compassionate protector, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, and ask for the <s>Dharma</s> that removes the fever of suffering. To them, the <s>Bhagavān</s>, having explained the cause under the name of 'origin' (<s>samudaya</s>), would prescribe the noble eightfold path as the great medicine that brings peace—<s>nirvāṇa</s>

(7) tatra bhikṣavaḥ katama āryāṣṭāṅgamārgaḥ? tadyathā - samyagdṛṣṭiḥ | samyaksaṃkalpaḥ | samyagvāk | samyakkarmāntaḥ | samyagājīvaḥ | samyagvyāyāmaḥ | samyaksmṛtiḥ | samyaksamādhiriti || tatra bhikṣavaḥ katamā samyagdṛṣṭiḥ? astyayaṃ lokaḥ, asti paralokaḥ, asti pitā, asti dattam, asti hutam, asti iṣṭāniṣṭasukṛtaduṣkṛtānāṃ karmaṇāṃ phalavipākaḥ, santi loke samyaggatāḥ samyakpratipannā iti | iyaṃ bhikṣavaḥ samyagdṛṣṭiḥ | samyaksaṃkalpaḥ katamaḥ? buddhatvādipariṇāmitaṃ dānam, śīlaṃ ca cakravartyādipariṇāmitam | ayaṃ bhikṣavaḥ samyaksaṃkalpaḥ || samyagvāk katamā? iha bhikṣavaḥ pāruṣyānṛtapaiśunyasaṃbhinnapralāpavarjitā anamṛtavāk | iyamucyate samyagvāk || samyakkarmāntaḥ katamaḥ? kāyavāṅmanasāṃ daśakuśaleṣu karmapatheṣu vyāpāraḥ | tatra kāyikaṃ trividham - prāṇātipātādadattādānātkāmamithyācārādviratiḥ | vācikaṃ caturvidham -

A monk, having consumed his alms-food, says again and again: "Such alms-food as this cannot be obtained in other lay households." But for one who speaks without a mind intent on gain and honor, there is no fault at all. This is called hinting (<s>naimittikatva</s>). Therein, what is intimidation (<s>naiṣpeṣikatva</s>)? A monk who does not receive alms-food in a certain household, but wishes to make them give, says there: "Non-givers go to hell. You too are non-givers; clearly you are bound for hell." Thus, out of those frightened by the terror of hell, he obtains alms-food, and having obtained it, he consumes it. This is called intimidation (<s>naiṣpeṣikatva</s>). Therein, what is seeking gain by means of gain (<s>lābhena lābhapratikāṅkṣā</s>)? A monk purchases fine robes with his own money and shows them to lay supporters, saying: "We receive such garments from our donors." Then they, impressed, give him garments, and he consumes them. This is called a monk's seeking gain by means of gain. This, monks, is wrong livelihood (<s>mithyājīva</s>); abstention from it is right livelihood (<s>samyagājīva</s>). Now, monks, what is wrong livelihood for a lay follower (<s>upāsaka</s>)? Selling poison, selling weapons, selling living beings, selling intoxicants, selling meat, and pressing sesame and mustard without proper inspection. This is a lay follower's wrong livelihood. Abstention from it—this is called, monks, right livelihood (<s>samyagājīva</s>). What is right effort (<s>samyagvyāyāma</s>)? Abundant bowing, attending, saluting with joined palms, and performing proper duties (<s>sāmīcīkarma</s>). This is called, monks, right effort (<s>samyagvyāyāma</s>). What is right mindfulness (<s>samyaksmṛti</s>)? Here, monks, a monk, having seen a woman and lust having arisen, contemplates with the aspect of the impure (<s>aśubha</s>) the true nature of both the external and internal bodies, [reflecting]: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, dust, impurity, skin, flesh, bones, sinews, veins, kidneys, heart, stomach lining, stomach, intestines, entrails, the excrement within, liver, waste matter, tears, sweat, saliva, mucus, fat, lymph, marrow, grease, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, brain matter, and urine—it is filled with various kinds of impurity." This is called, monks, right mindfulness (<s>samyaksmṛti</s>). What is right concentration (<s>samyaksamādhi</s>)? The four <s>dhyānas</s> (meditative absorptions). Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first <s>dhyāna</s>, which is accompanied by applied thought (<s>vitarka</s>) and sustained thought (<s>vicāra</s>), born of seclusion, filled with joy (<s>prīti</s>) and happiness (<s>sukha</s>). With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through inner tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, he attains and dwells in the second <s>dhyāna</s>, which is without applied thought and sustained thought, born of concentration, filled with joy and happiness. With the fading of joy, he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body. As the noble ones declare: "Equanimous, mindful, dwelling in happiness"—he attains and dwells in the third <s>dhyāna</s>. With the abandoning of happiness and suffering, and with the prior disappearance of mental pleasure and displeasure, he attains and dwells in the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, purified by equanimity and mindfulness. These, monks, are the four <s>dhyānas</s>. This is called right concentration (<s>samyaksamādhi</s>). This, monks, is called the noble eightfold path (<s>āryāṣṭāṅgamārga</s>).

body.translated_text: (7) 'Therein, monks, what is the noble eightfold path (<s>āryāṣṭāṅgamārga</s>)? They are: <s>samyagdṛṣṭi</s> (right view), <s>samyaksaṃkalpa</s> (right intention), <s>samyagvāk</s> (right speech), <s>samyakkarmānta</s> (right action), <s>samyagājīva</s> (right livelihood), <s>samyagvyāyāma</s> (right effort), <s>samyaksmṛti</s> (right mindfulness), <s>samyaksamādhi</s> (right concentration). Therein, monks, what is <s>samyagdṛṣṭi</s> (right view)? That this world exists, that the other world exists, that there is a father, that there is giving, that there is offering, that there is the fruit and ripening of good and bad actions, that there exist in the world those who have gone rightly and practiced rightly. This, monks, is <s>samyagdṛṣṭi</s>. What is <s>samyaksaṃkalpa</s> (right intention)? Giving dedicated toward Buddhahood and the like, and moral conduct dedicated toward becoming a <s>cakravartin</s> (universal monarch) and the like. This, monks, is <s>samyaksaṃkalpa</s>. What is <s>samyagvāk</s> (right speech)? Here, monks, speech that is free from harsh speech, lying, slander, and idle chatter—speech that is not false. This is called <s>samyagvāk</s>. What is <s>samyakkarmānta</s> (right action)? The engagement of body, speech, and mind in the ten wholesome courses of action (<s>kuśalakarmapatha</s>). Therein, the bodily kind is threefold: abstaining from taking life (<s>prāṇātipāta</s>), from taking what is not given (<s>adattādāna</s>), and from sexual misconduct (<s>kāmamithyācāra</s>). The verbal kind is fourfold: abstaining from lying (<s>anṛta</s>), harsh speech (<s>pāruṣya</s>), slander (<s>paiśunya</s>), and idle chatter (<s>saṃbhinnapralāpa</s>). The mental kind is threefold: abstaining from covetousness (<s>abhidhyā</s>), ill-will (<s>vyāpāda</s>), and wrong views (<s>mithyādṛṣṭi</s>). Therein, what is taking life? There is a living being, one perceives it as a living being, one generates the intention to kill, and one deprives it of life. This, monks, is called taking life—except for cases of negligence or not seeing, which do not constitute killing a living being. Therein, what is taking what is not given? The appropriation of another's property by one with the intention to steal is taking what is not given; except that taking a small amount from the property of one's mother, father, brother, relative, or friend without causing harm is also taking what is not given. Therein, what is sexual misconduct? The enjoyment of another's wife who is guarded by her husband, the king, or her mother and father; or else, engaging bodily in improper places, with improper persons, at improper times. Thus it is threefold. What is lying? In a witness inquiry, false testimony that is contrary to fact, or [saying] "I am an <s>arhat</s>" as an object of ridicule when it is not beneficial—this is called lying. What is slander? Speech that causes division, whether by falsehood or by truth, is slander. What is harsh speech? When one who desires to cause suffering to another makes another hear unpleasant words, with the thought "may this be suffering to him"—that making another hear cruel words is harsh speech. What is idle chatter? Talk about kings, talk about thieves, talk about gambling, talk about liquor, talk about women, talk about legends. This is called idle chatter. The verbal kind is thus fourfold. What is covetousness? With the desire to appropriate another's property, [thinking] "may those belongings of another be mine"—this is called covetousness. What is ill-will? Thinking about depriving another of life, cutting off, tormenting, and the like. This is called ill-will. What is wrong view? "This world does not exist, the other world does not exist," and so forth as before. This is the mental kind, which is threefold. This is called wrong view. Now, what is <s>samyagājīva</s> (right livelihood)? For a monk: hypocrisy (<s>kuhanā</s>), flattery (<s>lapanā</s>), hinting (<s>naimittikatva</s>), belittling (<s>naiṣpeṣikatva</s>), and seeking gain by means of gain—[abstaining from these] is right livelihood. Hypocrisy, flattery, and the rest [are defined as follows]. Therein, what is hypocrisy? A monk, seeing a patron, sits cross-legged on the road or in an empty dwelling, meditating—[thinking] "'The monk is an <s>arhat</s>'—thus gain and honor will come to me." Such and the like is called hypocrisy. Therein, what is flattery? Here a monk, solely for the sake of gain and honor, [says] "You are my mother, you are my daughter," and other such pleasant words

body.translated_text: (8) What are the twenty-two faculties (<s>indriya</s>)? Namely: the eye-faculty (<s>cakṣurindriya</s>), the ear-faculty (<s>śrotrendriya</s>), the nose-faculty (<s>ghrāṇendriya</s>), the tongue-faculty (<s>jihvendriya</s>), the body-faculty (<s>kāyendriya</s>), the mind-faculty (<s>manendriya</s>), the male faculty (<s>puruṣendriya</s>), the female faculty (<s>strīndriya</s>), the pain-faculty (<s>duḥkhendriya</s>), the pleasure-faculty (<s>sukhendriya</s>), the mental-pleasure-faculty (<s>saumanasyendriya</s>), the mental-displeasure-faculty (<s>daurmanasyendriya</s>), the equanimity-faculty (<s>upekṣendriya</s>), the faith-faculty (<s>śraddhendriya</s>), the energy-faculty (<s>vīryendriya</s>), the concentration-faculty (<s>samādhīndriya</s>), the mindfulness-faculty (<s>smṛtīndriya</s>), the knowledge-faculty (<s>jñānendriya</s>), the life-faculty (<s>jīvitendriya</s>), the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (<s>anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya</s>), the faculty of perfect knowledge (<s>ājñendriya</s>), and the faculty of one who has fully known (<s>ājñātāvīndriya</s>). These, monks, are the twenty-two faculties.

children.translated_text: ) (9) 'Therein, monks, what are the four <s>dhyānas</s> (meditative absorptions)? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome <s>dharma</s>s, having applied thought (<s>vitarka</s>) and sustained thought (<s>vicāra</s>), [experiencing] the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters and dwells in the first <s>dhyāna</s>. With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through inner tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, without applied thought and without sustained thought, [experiencing] the joy and happiness born of <s>samādhi</s> (concentration), he enters and dwells in the second <s>dhyāna</s>. Through the fading away of joy, he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness through the body — that which the noble ones declare: "equanimous, mindful, dwelling in happiness" — he enters and dwells in the third <s>dhyāna</s>. Through the abandoning of happiness and the abandoning of suffering, and with the prior disappearance of mental pleasure and mental displeasure, he enters and dwells in the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>, which is neither suffering nor happiness, purified by equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>) and mindfulness (<s>smṛti</s>). These, monks, are the four <s>dhyānas</s>.'

body.text: (10) tatra katame catvāro brahmavihārāḥ? iha bhikṣavo bhikṣurmaitrīsahagatena cittena avaireṇa asaṃpannena avyābādhena vipulena mahadgatena apramāṇena subhāvitena ekādrisamaṃ vimucya sphuritvā upasaṃpadya viharati, tathā dvitīyam, tathā tṛtīyam, tathā caturtham, iti ūrdhvamadhastiryak sarvaśaḥ sarvāvantamimaṃ lokaṃ maitrīsahagatena cittena avaireṇa asaṃpannena avyābādhena vipulena mahadgatena advayena apramāṇena subhāvitena ekāṃ diśamadhimucya sphuritvā upasaṃpadya viharati | evaṃ karuṇāsahagatena, muditāsahagatena, upekṣāsahagatena cittena avaireṇa asaṃpannena avyābādhena vipulena mahadgatena advayena apramāṇena subhāvitena ekāṃ diśamadhimucya sphuritvā upasaṃpadya viharati | ime catvāro brahmavihārāḥ ||
body.translated_text: (10) 'Therein, what are the four <s>brahmavihāras</s> (divine abodes)? Here, monks, a monk dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness (<s>maitrī</s>), free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from harm, vast, great, immeasurable, well-cultivated, releasing and pervading [all] as if encompassing a single mountain, he enters and dwells [therein]; likewise the second [direction], likewise the third, likewise the fourth — thus above, below, across, in every direction, the entire world — he dwells having pervaded with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from harm, vast, great, non-dual, immeasurable, well-cultivated, releasing and pervading one direction, he enters and dwells [therein]. Likewise with a mind accompanied by compassion (<s>karuṇā</s>), with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy (<s>muditā</s>), with a mind accompanied by equanimity (<s>upekṣā</s>), free from enmity, free from ill-will, free from harm, vast, great, non-dual, immeasurable, well-cultivated, releasing and pervading one direction, he enters and dwells [therein]. These are the four <s>brahmavihāras</s>.'

Furthermore, monks, a monk should examine this body in terms of its primary and secondary causes. The primary cause of this body is its arising from the seed and blood of mother and father. The secondary [cause] is the measure of food and so forth. Morsel-food (<s>kavalikāhāra</s>), once swallowed, goes to the seat of phlegm (<s>śleṣmāśaya</s>). Having reached the seat of phlegm, being liquefied by phlegm, it becomes utterly impure. From the phlegm it goes to the seat of bile (<s>pittāśaya</s>). Having reached the seat of bile, being cooked and becoming heated, it goes to the seat of wind (<s>vāyvāśaya</s>). Having been cooked and reaching the seat of wind, it is separated by wind—the waste apart, the essence apart. From the waste come urine, feces, and other impurities. From the essence, blood (<s>śoṇita</s>) is transformed; from blood, flesh (<s>māṃsa</s>); from flesh, fat (<s>medas</s>); from fat, bones (<s>asthi</s>); from bones, marrow (<s>majjā</s>); from marrow, semen (<s>śukra</s>). Thus, a monk who sees the body as impure due to primary and secondary causes [should understand that] this body is raised up by nine hundred and sixty bones, like a poorly-built wooden house; joined together by three hundred joints; bound by four hundred networks of veins; plastered over by five hundred bundles of flesh; bent by seven hundred sinews; fastened by nine hundred ligaments; pierced through by arteries like windows; fragile like a broken vessel with one hundred and seven vital points; covered like grass by eighty hundred-thousand millions [of hairs]; with five sense openings; filled with impurity in seven receptacles—with a handful of brain, a handful of fat, three handfuls of grease, six handfuls of phlegm, six handfuls of bile, all drawn through by wind; filled separately and equally with a measure of blood and six measures of feces; wrapped in seven layers of skin, with six flavors; the fire of the body, possessed by the fire of bile and wind, like a constantly burning sacrificial fire (?), the body with all its parts is indeed foul-looking, foul-smelling by its very nature. What conceit or pride can there be here? It is to be borne only like borrowed goods for momentary use, like a cart for carrying loads—with the understanding of <s>Dharma</s>.

body.translated_text: Thus one contemplates and so forth. Just as, monks, a granary with doors open on both sides, filled with various kinds of grain—sesame, mustard, mung beans, barley, and black beans—and a man with good eyesight, looking at it, would know: 'these are husked grains, these are seed grains.' Just so, monks, the monk contemplates this very body as it is positioned, as it is disposed. This cultivation of <s>samādhi</s> (concentration), when practiced and developed, conduces to the abandoning of sensual desire (<s>kāmarāga</s>). Therein, monks, what cultivation of <s>samādhi</s>, when practiced, developed, and much cultivated, conduces to pleasant abiding in the present life (<s>dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra</s>)? Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, suffuses, fills, saturates, and pervades this very body internally, personally, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion. There is nothing of his entire body that is not pervaded, not suffused by the internally-born joy and happiness of seclusion. Just as, monks, blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, or pink lotuses, born in the water and submerged in the water, are all suffused, permeated, filled, saturated, and pervaded by the cool water; just so, a monk, having gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, suffuses, permeates, fills, pervades, and saturates this very body internally, personally, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion. There is nothing of his entire body that is not pervaded, not suffused by the internal joy and happiness born of seclusion. This cultivation of <s>samādhi</s>, when practiced, developed, and much cultivated, conduces to pleasant abiding in the present life. Therein, monks, what cultivation of <s>samādhi</s>, when practiced, developed, and much cultivated, conduces to the attainment of knowledge and vision (<s>jñānadarśana</s>)? Here, monks, the perception of light (<s>ālokasaṃjñā</s>) is well and thoroughly grasped by the monk, well attended to, well seen, and well secured. He cultivates a mind established in the perception of daylight, with equal radiance—as by day so by night, as by night so by day; as before so after, as after so before; as below so above, as above so below. With an open mind, unobstructed, he cultivates a mind established in the perception of daylight, with equal radiance. Just so, monks, the perception of light is well and thoroughly grasped by the monk, well attended to, well secured. He cultivates a mind established in the perception of daylight, with equal radiance—as by day so by night, as by night so by day; as before so after, as after so before; as above so below, as below so above. With an open mind, unobstructed, he cultivates a mind established in the perception of daylight, with equal radiance. body.text: [13] tatra katamāni bhikṣavaścatvāri smṛtyupasthānāni? iha bhikṣavo bhikṣuradhyātmaṃ kāye kāyānudarśī viharati ātāpī saṃprajānan smṛtimān vinīya loke abhidhyādaurmanasye | bahirdhā kāye kāyānudarśī viharati, adhyātmabahirdhā kāye kāyānudarśī viharati ātāpī saṃprajānan anusmṛtimān vinīya loke abhidhyādaurmanasye | adhyātmavadenāsu bahirdhāvedanāsu adhyātmabahirdhā vedanāsu vedanānudarśī viharati ātāpī saṃprajānan smṛtimān vinīya loke abhidhyādaurmanasye | adhyātmacitte bahirdhācitte adhyātmabahirdhā cittānudarśī viharati ātāpī saṃprajānan smṛtimān vinīya loke abhidhyādaurmanasye | adhyātmadharmeṣu bahirdhādharmeṣu adhyātmabahirdhādharmeṣu dharmānudarśī viharati ātāpī saṃprajānan smṛtimān vinīya loke abhidhyādaurmanasye | itīmāni catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni ||
body.translated_text: [13] 'Therein, monks, what are the four <s>smṛtyupasthānas</s> (foundations of mindfulness)? Here, monks, a monk dwells observing the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and mental distress regarding the world. He dwells observing the body in the body externally; he dwells observing the body in the body both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and mental distress regarding the world. He dwells observing feelings in feelings internally, externally, and both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and mental distress regarding the world. He dwells observing the mind in the mind internally, externally, and both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and mental distress regarding the world. He dwells observing <s>dharmas</s> in <s>dharmas</s> internally, externally, and both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and mental distress regarding the world. These are the four foundations of mindfulness.'

body.text: [14] tatra katamāni bhikṣavaścatvāri samyakprahāṇāni? iha bhikṣavo bhikṣuranutpannānāṃ pāpakānāmakuśalānāṃ dharmāṇāmanutpādāya chandaṃ janayati, vyāyacchati, vīryamārabhate, cittaṃ saṃpratigṛhṇāti, samyak praṇidadhāti | utpannānāmakuśalānāṃ dharmāṇāṃ prahāṇāya chandaṃ janayati, vyāyacchati, vīryamārabhate, cittaṃ pragṛhṇāti, saṃpraṇidadhāti | anutpannānāṃ kuśalānāṃ dharmāṇāmutpādāya chandaṃ janayati, vyāyacchati, vīryamārabhate, cittaṃ pragṛhṇāti, samyak praṇidadhāti | utpannānāṃ kuśalānāṃ dharmāṇāṃ sthitaye bhāvanāyai asaṃmoṣāya aparihāṇāya bhūyobhāvāya vṛddhivipulatāyai pāripūryai chandaṃ janayati, vyāyacchati, vīryamārabhate, cittaṃ pratigṛhṇāti samyak praṇidadhāti | imāni catvāri samyakprahāṇāni ||
body.translated_text: [14] 'Therein, monks, what are the four <s>samyakprahāṇas</s> (right exertions)? Here, monks, a monk generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome <s>dharmas</s>; he exerts himself, arouses vigor, takes hold of the mind, and rightly resolves. He generates desire for the abandoning of arisen unwholesome <s>dharmas</s>; he exerts himself, arouses vigor, takes hold of the mind, and rightly resolves. He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome <s>dharmas</s>; he exerts himself, arouses vigor, takes hold of the mind, and rightly resolves. He generates desire for the maintenance, cultivation, non-confusion, non-decline, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome <s>dharmas</s>; he exerts himself, arouses vigor, takes hold of the mind, and rightly resolves. These are the four right exertions.'

body.text: [15] tatra katame catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ? iha bhikṣavo bhikṣuḥ chandasamādhiprahāṇasaṃskārasamanvāgatamṛddhipādaṃ bhāvayati vivekaniśritaṃ virāganiśritaṃ nirodhaniśritaṃ vyavasargapariṇatam | eṣā............vīryamabhilīnaṃ bhaviṣyati nābhigṛhītam ||2 || cittasamādhiprahāṇasaṃskārasamanvāgatamṛddhipādaṃ bhāvayati vivekaniśritaṃ virāganiśritaṃ nirodhaniśritaṃ vyavasargapariṇataṃ mā me cittamatilīnaṃ bhaviṣyati nābhigṛhītam ||3 || mīmāṃsāsamādhiprahāṇasaṃskārasamanvāgatamṛddhipādaṃ bhāvayati vivekaniśritaṃ virāganiśritaṃ nirodhaniśritaṃ vyavasargapariṇataṃ mā me mīmāṃsā nātilīnā bhaviṣyati nābhigṛhītam ||4 || ime bhikṣavaścatvāra ṛddhipādāḥ ||
body.translated_text: [15] 'Therein, what are the four <s>ṛddhipādas</s> (bases of supernatural power)? Here, monks, a monk cultivates the basis of supernatural power endowed with concentration born of desire and the formations of exertion (<s>chandasamādhiprahāṇasaṃskāra</s>), based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. [...] [2] He cultivates the basis of supernatural power endowed with concentration born of vigor and the formations of exertion, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment — [thinking:] "May my vigor not become too lax nor too tense." [3] He cultivates the basis of supernatural power endowed with concentration born of mind (<s>citta</s>) and the formations of exertion, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment — [thinking:] "May my mind not become too lax nor too tense." [4] He cultivates the basis of supernatural power endowed with concentration born of investigation (<s>mīmāṃsā</s>) and the formations of exertion, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment — [thinking:] "May my investigation not become too lax nor too tense." These, monks, are the four bases of supernatural power.'

body.translated_text: [17] Therein, monks, what are the five powers (<s>pañcabala</s>)? body.translated_text: [18] Therein, monks, what are the seven factors of awakening (<s>sapta bodhyaṅga</s>)? Namely: the awakening factor of mindfulness (<s>smṛtisaṃbodhyaṅga</s>), the awakening factor of investigation of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga</s>), the awakening factor of energy (<s>vīryasaṃbodhyaṅga</s>), the awakening factor of joy (<s>prītisaṃbodhyaṅga</s>), the awakening factor of tranquility (<s>prasrabdhisaṃbodhyaṅga</s>), the awakening factor of concentration (<s>samādhisaṃbodhyaṅga</s>), and the awakening factor of equanimity (<s>upekṣāsaṃbodhyaṅga</s>). Here, monks, a monk cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, based on seclusion (<s>viveka</s>), based on dispassion (<s>virāga</s>), based on cessation (<s>nirodha</s>), maturing in relinquishment (<s>vyavasarga</s>). Likewise, he cultivates the awakening factor of investigation of <s>dharmas</s>, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He cultivates the awakening factor of energy, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He cultivates the awakening factor of joy, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He cultivates the awakening factor of tranquility, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He cultivates the awakening factor of concentration, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He cultivates the awakening factor of equanimity, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. These, monks, are the seven factors of awakening.

body.text: [19] tatra bhikṣavaḥ katama āryāṣṭāṅga(mārgaḥ)? tadyathā - samyagdṛṣṭiḥ samyaksaṃkalpaḥ samyagvāk samyakkarmāntaḥ samyagājīvaḥ samyagvyāyāmaḥ samyaksmṛtiḥ samyaksamādhiḥ | ayamucyate bhikṣava āryāṣṭāṅgamārgaḥ || tatra katamā samyagdṛṣṭiḥ? yā lokottarā nātmadṛṣṭisamutthitā na sa.........najīvan soṣaṇapuruṣanapudgalanamanujanamānavadṛṣṭisamutthitā nocchedaśāśvatadṛṣṭisamutthitā na bhavavibhavadṛṣṭisamutthitā na kuśalāvyākṛtadṛṣṭisamutthitā, yā ca na saṃsāranirvāṇadṛṣṭisamutthitā | iyamucyate samyagdṛṣṭiḥ || tatra katamaḥ samyaksaṃkalyaḥ? yaiḥ saṃkalpai rāgadveṣa mohakleśāḥ samuttiṣṭhanti, tān saṃkalpān na saṃkalpayati | yaiḥ(saṃ)kalpaiḥ śīlasamādhiprajñā vimuktidarśanaskandhāḥ samuttiṣṭhanti, tān saṃkalpān saṃkalpayati | ayamucyate samyaksaṃkalpaḥ ||
body.translated_text: [19] Therein, monks, what is the noble eightfold path (<s>āryāṣṭāṅgamārga</s>)? Namely: right view (<s>samyagdṛṣṭi</s>), right intention (<s>samyaksaṃkalpa</s>), right speech (<s>samyagvāk</s>), right action (<s>samyakkarmānta</s>), right livelihood (<s>samyagājīva</s>), right effort (<s>samyagvyāyāma</s>), right mindfulness (<s>samyaksmṛti</s>), and right concentration (<s>samyaksamādhi</s>). This is called, monks, the noble eightfold path. Therein, what is right view (<s>samyagdṛṣṭi</s>)? That which is supramundane (<s>lokottara</s>), not arisen from the view of self (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>), not arisen from views of a soul (<s>jīva</s>), a being, a person (<s>pudgala</s>), a human, or a man; not arisen from the views of annihilation (<s>uccheda</s>) or eternalism (<s>śāśvata</s>); not arisen from views of existence or non-existence (<s>bhava</s>, <s>vibhava</s>); not arisen from views of wholesome or indeterminate [states]; and that which is not arisen from views of <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence) or <s>nirvāṇa</s>. This is called right view. Therein, what is right intention (<s>samyaksaṃkalpa</s>)? Those intentions by which the defilements of passion (<s>rāga</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), and delusion (<s>moha</s>) arise—those intentions one does not intend. Those intentions by which the aggregates of moral conduct (<s>śīla</s>), concentration (<s>samādhi</s>), wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>), liberation (<s>vimukti</s>), and the knowledge and vision of liberation arise—those intentions one intends. This is called right intention.

children.translated_text: He does not perform that action which has dark-and-bright ripening; he performs that action which conduces to the destruction of all <s>karma</s> (<s>kṛṣṇakarmakṣaya</s>). He performs wholesome action; his action is founded on wholesome action. This is called <s>samyakkarmānta</s> (right action). Therein, what is <s>samyagājīva</s> (right livelihood)? That which, for the sake of meaning, involves the letting go of attachment to qualities—without hypocrisy (<s>kuhanā</s>), without flattery (<s>lapanā</s>), without belittling (<s>naiṣpeṣikatā</s>), the habit of flowing speech, fear regarding other worlds, contentment with one's own world, freedom from decline, the livelihood known among the noble ones. This is called <s>samyagājīva</s>. Therein, what is <s>samyagvyāyāma</s> (right effort)? That effort which is wrong, which is accompanied by ignorance, passion, aversion, delusion, and the latent defilements (<s>anuśaya</s>)—that effort one does not desire. That effort which is right, which reveals entry into the noble path and truth, which leads to <s>nirvāṇa</s>—that effort one follows. This is called <s>samyagvyāyāma</s>. Therein, what is <s>samyaksmṛti</s> (right mindfulness)? That mindfulness which is well-established, unshakable, straight, not crooked, which sees the faults of <s>saṃsāra</s> with revulsion, which leads to the path of <s>nirvāṇa</s>—a pervading, a non-forgetting of the noble path. This is called <s>samyaksmṛti</s>. Therein, what is <s>samyaksamādhi</s> (right concentration)? That concentration which is by way of rightness. That concentration in which, being established, one rightly enters the certainty (<s>niyāma</s>) of firm abiding for the liberation of all beings. This is called <s>samyaksamādhi</s>. This is called the noble eightfold path (<s>āryāṣṭāṅgamārga</s>).'

[21] tatra katamāni catvāri srotaāpattyaṅgāni? iha bhikṣavaḥ śrāvako 'vetya buddhe prasādena samanvāgato bhavati - ityapi sa bhagavāṃstathāgato 'rhan samyaksaṃbuddho vidyācaraṇasaṃpannaḥ sugato lokavidanuttaraḥ puruṣadamyasārathiḥ śāstā devamanuṣyāṇāṃ buddho bhagavāniti | dharme 'vetya prasādena samanvāgato bhavati - svākhyāto bhagavatā dharmaḥ sāṃdṛṣṭiko nirjvaraḥ ākālika aupanāyikaḥ ihapaśyakaḥ pratyātmavedanīyo vijñairyaduta nadanimadanapadheyāsāṃ(?) prativinaya ālayasamuddhāto dharmopacchedaḥ śūnyatānupalambhaḥ tṛṣṇākṣayo nirodho nirvāṇam | saṃghe 'vetya prasādena samanvāgato bhavati - supratipanno bhagavataḥ āryaśrāvakasaṃgho nyāyapratipannaḥ sapratipannaḥ sāmīcipratipanno dharmānudharmapratipanno 'nudharmacārī | santi saṃghe srotāpattiphalasākṣātkriyāyai pratipannakāḥ | santi saṃghe srotāpannaḥ | santi saṃghe sakṛdāgāmiphalasākṣātkriyāyai pratipannakāḥ | santi saṃghe sakṛdāgāminaḥ

body.translated_text: [21] Therein, what are the four factors of stream-entry (<s>srotaāpattyaṅga</s>)? Here, monks, a disciple (<s>śrāvaka</s>) is endowed with unwavering faith in the <s>Buddha</s>: 'Thus indeed is the <s>Bhagavān</s>, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the <s>Arhat</s>, the Perfectly Enlightened One (<s>Samyaksaṃbuddha</s>), endowed with knowledge and conduct (<s>vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna</s>), the Well-Gone One (<s>Sugata</s>), the Knower of the World (<s>Lokavid</s>), the Unsurpassed, the Charioteer of Persons to be Tamed (<s>Puruṣadamyasārathi</s>), the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the <s>Buddha</s>, the <s>Bhagavān</s>.' He is endowed with unwavering faith in the <s>Dharma</s>: 'Well-proclaimed is the <s>Dharma</s> of the <s>Bhagavān</s> — visible here and now, free from torment, timeless, inviting one to come and see, to be personally experienced by the wise — namely: the discipline that removes this and that affliction, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of <s>dharmas</s>, emptiness, non-apprehension, the exhaustion of craving, cessation, <s>nirvāṇa</s>.' He is endowed with unwavering faith in the <s>Saṃgha</s>: 'Well-practiced is the noble community of disciples of the <s>Bhagavān</s> — practicing the right way, practicing the proper way, practicing the fitting way, practicing in accordance with the <s>Dharma</s>, following the <s>Dharma</s>. There are in the <s>Saṃgha</s> those practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (<s>srotāpattiphala</s>). There are in the <s>Saṃgha</s> stream-enterers (<s>srotāpanna</s>). There are in the <s>Saṃgha</s> those practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning (<s>sakṛdāgāmiphala</s>). There are in the <s>Saṃgha</s> once-returners (<s>sakṛdāgāmin</s>). There are in the <s>Saṃgha</s> those practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning (<s>anāgāmiphala</s>). There are in the <s>Saṃgha</s> non-returners (<s>anāgāmin</s>). There are in the <s>Saṃgha</s> those practicing for the realization of the fruit of <s>arhatship</s> (<s>arhattvaphala</s>). There are in the <s>Saṃgha</s> <s>arhats</s>. That is, four pairs of persons, eight individual persons. This community of disciples of the <s>Bhagavān</s> is endowed with faith, endowed with learning, endowed with <s>samādhi</s> (concentration), endowed with wisdom (<s>prajñā</s>), endowed with liberation (<s>vimukti</s>), endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation (<s>vimuktijñānadarśana</s>) — worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world, worthy of being seen — namely, endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones: virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unspotted, unmottled, untainted, free, unpolluted, well-assembled, praised by the wise, leading to victory, blameless according to the wise.' These are the four factors of stream-entry.

body.translated_text: [23] 'What, monks, are the four <s>vaiśāradyas</s> (fearlessnesses) of the <s>Tathāgata</s>? Here, the <s>Bhagavān</s> knows himself to be a <s>samyaksaṃbuddha</s> (perfectly awakened one). Should anyone bring the charge: "These <s>dharmas</s> have not been awakened to by you"—in this world with its gods, <s>Māra</s>, and <s>Brahmā</s>, among the generations with <s>śramaṇas</s> and <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, gods and humans—he sees no basis [for such a charge]. Seeing no such basis, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the <s>Bhagavān</s>, attains security, attains fearlessness, knows the position of the bull. Having rightly entered the assembly, he roars the lion's roar. He sets in motion the <s>Brahma</s>-wheel, which has not been set in motion by any <s>śramaṇa</s> or <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, god or <s>Māra</s>, or by anyone else in the world, in accordance with the <s>Dharma</s>. Furthermore, regarding those <s>dharmas</s> declared by the <s>Tathāgata</s> as obstructive—should anyone bring the charge that practicing them would not obstruct [progress]—and so forth in detail. And the path declared by him as noble, leading to liberation—should anyone bring the charge that following it, giving up the lower, one would not reach liberation, nor the complete cessation of suffering... [the same pattern as before]. For one who declares himself to have destroyed the <s>āsravas</s>—should anyone bring the charge: "These <s>āsravas</s> are not destroyed"—in this world with its gods, <s>Māra</s>, and <s>Brahmā</s>, among the generations with <s>śramaṇas</s> and <s>brāhmaṇas</s>, gods and humans—he sees no such basis. Not seeing such a basis, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, having attained strength, dwells fearless, knows the position of the bull. Having rightly entered the assembly, he roars the lion's roar, sets in motion the <s>Brahma</s>-wheel, which has not been set in motion by any <s>śramaṇa</s> or <s>brāhmaṇa</s> or by anyone else in the world, in accordance with the <s>Dharma</s>. These, monks, are the four <s>vaiśāradyas</s> (fearlessnesses) of the <s>Bhagavān</s>, the <s>Tathāgata</s>.'

Having a voice like <s>Brahmā</s> and the <s>kalaviṅka</s> bird (<s>brahmakalaviṅkarutasvaratā</s>)—this mark of a great being (<s>mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa</s>) of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced through speaking affectionate words to beings and through causing them to hear words of joy in past lives. Having deep blue eyes (<s>abhinīlanetratā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through protecting beings with loving-kindness (<s>maitrī</s>) in past lives. Having eyelashes like a cow (<s>gopakṣmanetratā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through not [acting with] artifice in past lives. Having a fine complexion (<s>sūkṣmacchavitā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through guarding the mind in <s>Dharma</s> assemblies (<s>dharmasaṃgīti</s>) and through pliancy of mind in past lives. Having a golden-colored complexion (<s>suvarṇavarṇacchavitā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through the gift of bedding, seats, coverings, and pleasant words in past lives. Having one hair in each pore (<s>ekaikaromakūpatā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through avoiding crowded gatherings (<s>saṃgaṇikā</s>) in past lives. Having body-hairs that curl to the right (<s>pradakṣiṇāvartaromatā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through respectfully receiving the instructions of teachers (<s>ācārya</s>), preceptors (<s>upādhyāya</s>), and good spiritual friends (<s>kalyāṇamitra</s>) in past lives. Having hair the color of indigo (<s>indranīlakeśatā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through compassion for all living beings and through having laid down clods, sticks, and weapons in past lives. Having a bright white <s>ūrṇā</s> (tuft of hair) between the eyebrows on the forehead (<s>suśuklabhramukhāntarorṇalalāṭatā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through speaking praise of those worthy of praise in past lives. Having the <s>uṣṇīṣa</s> (crown protuberance) on the head (<s>uṣṇīṣaśiraskatā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through bowing respectfully to elders and teachers in past lives. Having a body symmetrical like the <s>nyagrodha</s> tree, pleasing on all sides (<s>nyagrodhaparimaṇḍalasamantaprāsādikatā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through engaging oneself and other beings in <s>samādhi</s> (concentration) in past lives. Having a body pleasing on all sides (<s>śarīrasamantaprāsādikatā</s>)—this mark of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced through making images of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, repairing broken <s>stūpas</s>, and giving reassurance and consolation to those who were frightened in past lives. Through immeasurable roots of merit and through mastery over those <s>dharmas</s>, the thirty-two marks of a great being (<s>dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa</s>) have been produced on the body of the <s>Tathāgata</s>.

body.translated_text: [26] 'Therein, what are the thirty-two marks of a great being (<s>dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa</s>) of the <s>Tathāgata</s>? Well-established feet—this is a mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being. Wheel-marked soles on the underside of both feet. Elongated heels with joined feet. Long fingers. Webbed hands and feet. Soft and tender hands and feet. Seven prominent parts of the body. Antelope-like calves. Male organ concealed in a sheath. Lion-like front of the body. Full between the shoulders. Well-rounded shoulders. Erect stature. Arms reaching to the knees. Pure eyes. Conch-shell neck. Lion jaw. Even forty teeth. Even and gapless teeth. Very white teeth. Long and thin tongue. Supreme sense of taste. A voice like <s>Brahmā</s> and the song of the <s>kalaviṅka</s> bird. Deep blue eyes. Cow-eyelash eyes. Fine complexion. Golden-colored complexion. One hair per pore. Hairs curving upward to the right. Hair dark as indigo. A white <s>ūrṇā</s> (tuft of hair) between the eyebrows on the forehead. An <s>uṣṇīṣa</s> (protuberance) on the head. Proportions like a <s>nyagrodha</s> (banyan) tree, pleasant on all sides. Strength of the great <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>, pleasant on all sides. This is a mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being. These, monks, are the marks of a great being of the <s>Tathāgata</s>. Well-established feet—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced formerly through firm undertaking. Wheel-marked soles on the underside of both feet—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced formerly through not causing crookedness in other beings. Elongated heels with joined feet—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s> was produced formerly through honoring mother and father and serving at their feet. Long fingers—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced formerly through guarding, protecting, and defending the <s>Dharma</s>. Webbed hands and feet—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced formerly through not dividing one's retinue. Soft and tender hands and feet—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced formerly through giving various coverings and food. Seven prominent parts of the body—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced through showing a willing face toward the needs of others. [...] Pure eyes—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced formerly through firm undertaking of the ten wholesome courses of action (<s>daśakuśalakarmapatha</s>). Conch-shell neck—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced formerly through giving various medicines and food to the sick. Lion jaw—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced formerly through the practice of wholesome roots (<s>kuśalamūla</s>). Even forty teeth—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced formerly through the practice of consoling beings. Gapless teeth—this mark of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, the great being, was produced formerly through reuniting divided beings. body.translated_text: As the <s>Bhagavān</s> has said: 'I shall teach you the <s>Dharma</s>, monks — beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, beautiful at the end, good in meaning, good in expression; I shall make known the holy life (<s>brahmacarya</s>) that is complete, fulfilled, pure, and stainless — namely, the discourse called the <s>Arthaviniścaya</s> (Ascertainment of Meaning).' Since that which was stated has now been explained: 'Monks, in forest dwellings, empty houses, mountain caves, ravines, grass huts, open spaces, charnel grounds, forest clearings ......... monks, do not be heedless! Do not become those who regret afterwards! This is our instruction.'

body.translated_text: When this discourse (<s>dharmaparyāya</s>) was being spoken, the minds of five hundred monks were liberated from the <s>āsravas</s> (defilements).

body.translated_text: Thus spoke the <s>Bhagavān</s>. Those monks, delighted in mind, and the entire assembly together with the world of gods (<s>deva</s>), humans (<s>mānuṣa</s>), <s>asuras</s>, and <s>gandharvas</s> rejoiced at the words of the <s>Bhagavān</s>.
